subject: Critical Thinking
title: Base Rate Neglect: Ignoring the Background Numbers
description: Learn Base Rate Neglect: Ignoring the Background Numbers in one minute.

hook.text: A test is 99% accurate. You test positive for a rare disease. What's the chance you actually have it?

buildup.text: Base rate neglect: ignoring how common something is in the general population when evaluating evidence.

discovery.text: If a disease affects 1 in 10,000 and the test has 1% false positives, ~99 false alarms occur for every true case.

twist.text: Doctors fall for this too. Studies show physicians dramatically overestimate the meaning of positive test results.

climax.text: Bayes' Theorem is the mathematical fix — it forces you to factor in the base rate before updating beliefs.

quiz.question: Why can a 99% accurate test still produce mostly false positives?
options: If the condition is rare, false positives vastly outnumber true positives
The math doesn't apply to medicine

details.summary: Base rate neglect occurs when you ignore general statistical information in favor of specific but less reliable information. A positive test result feels definitive, but without knowing the base rate of the condition, you cannot interpret it correctly.
details.whyItMatters: Base rate neglect causes medical misdiagnoses, false accusations, and poor risk assessment whenever vivid individual data overshadows statistical context.
takeaways: Base rates set the statistical background for any individual case
Vivid specific information crowds out boring but crucial statistics
Bayesian reasoning corrects for base rate neglect

faq.question: How does base rate neglect affect medical testing interpretations?
faq.answer: If a disease affects 1 in 10,000 people and a test has a 1% false positive rate, a positive result is still far more likely to be a false positive. Without the base rate, patients and doctors overestimate the diagnosis certainty.

faq.question: What is the simplest way to avoid base rate neglect in daily decisions?
faq.answer: Always ask: how common is this in the general population? Before interpreting any specific result, establish the background frequency. This one question corrects many instances of base rate neglect.
